Was a distinction made between the facts and their personal opinions?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We made a point of distinguishing between facts and assessment. Now, when you read the various reports, especially the kind of reports which are termed "political excerpts," you will see that that dividing line is not always easy to find. One reason is the difference in background. Some of the monitors were fairly young officers or reserve officers; some were fairly senior, be from the level of 1st Lieutenant to Colonel, on the monitor side; and they were military men. The diplomats or civilians who were there would rank from a young first secretary to an Ambassador. So there was a huge difference in background of the people. There was also a difference in command of English, English being the language of the mission. It is fairly obvious from the reports which have been brought into evidence in the court. So, yes, it was the opinion of the mission that there should be made a distinction between facts and assessment. In practice it was sometimes difficult to uphold that distinction for the reasons I mentioned, coupled in some cases also with pure fatigue, because many of these people were working very, very long hours under difficult circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And to complete my question -- Mr. Mikulicic, I do apologise to you -- a certain level of this European mission were there to established facts, to find the facts. You received the information, but before you make your report do you try to go through all the information and, therefore, gather it, infiltrate in order to produce a report on facts?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have different reports before us. The mundane reporting system was based on the fact that every team reported at the end of every day what they had done for the whole of the day. That would include political talks, whatever military establishments they had visited, monitoring of weapons in storage in some cases, monitoring of ceasefire lines, simple questions as to their logistics, et cetera. These reports would be sent to the coordination centre, which would compile a combined report based on the various team reports. That again would be sent to the RC, which would again condense the report before sending it off to Zagreb. Now in Zagreb, the chief of operations and his people in the operations centre would compile a draft daily report which would be sent over to Copenhagen after it had been reviewed by the political advisor, by the chief of staff, by myself, and ultimately shown to the head of the mission before we sent it to Copenhagen. In Copenhagen it would again be looked over by a desk officer and then disseminated to the capitals of the European Union and with copies made to the co-chairmen, Vance and Owen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these reports that you are referring to, what kind of reports were they? Were they internal reports or were they public reports; that is, reports that could perhaps be published and given to the media?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reports that were made were internal in the sense that they would, probably all of them, be marked ECMM restricted. That means that they were not for publication. They were meant for the next higher level in command, and they were ultimately to be distributed to the member states of the European Union. Only if they were marked "press communiqué", or whatever, would they be made available to the public, not the regular reporting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I understand it, the reports which were shown to be ECMM restricted, they were meant for restrictive use only. Who would be the individual who would authorise giving such reports to anyone outside the ECMM, who had such an authority?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on who you would give the report to. If you give it to the co-chairman, the liaison officer, would, of course, be authorised to do so. If it was to the U.N., UNPROFOR, yes, of course, the liaison officers could do it. If we're talking about the public, meaning the media, such decisions would normally have to be taken by a person who was confident that he could take that responsibility. What I'm trying to say is that there were no written-down, formal, legal, strict rules on the dissemination of these reports. But again when they were marked restricted, they were not intended to be made public, but they could be distributed to friendly agencies and governments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move on to another topic, Mr. Brix Andersen. We shall be helped, I believe, by a map, and I should like to ask the usher to help me to distribute it and show it to you. It is about the position of the Croat national minority in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, what is the map that you're showing the witness, and where is it from, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This map is showing the ethnic composition of the municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina based on the 1991 census, and the map was used as a Prosecution exhibit in the Aleksovski case, produced through the expert witness Professor Bianchini.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Anderson, we spoke about the Croat community or Croats, if you will, in the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. On this map, the Croats are in red. However, if you look at this map, then you will see that in three -- that Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina are grouped in three areas; in the north in the municipalities of Bosanski Brod and others; then in Central Bosnia there is municipalities of Vitez, Busovaca, and so forth; and in south-west Bosnia, that is the municipalities bordering on south-east Croatia. Now, my question is, and I'm referring to the ECMM mission, in your view was the ECMM aware of the difference between individual -- were you aware of the fact that various Croat communities in Bosnia-Herzegovina did not always share the interests, bearing in mind their geographical location and the surroundings and environment in which they lived?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you rephrase that question for my better understanding?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I do apologise for not being clear enough. So Mr. Andersen, my question is the following: Did the ECMM see the Croat community in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as an integral and uniform community, in view of the geographic location, but did it also perceive that there were differences between individual Croat communities, in view of their geographical location?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were aware of the 1991 census. We knew of these figures. We knew the approximate distribution of the various ethnic groups in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We also knew, as is clear from this point of the report in evidence here, that the wishes and aspirations and interests of the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina were not always the very same, depending on where in Bosnia they were located. That is true. You will see one of the reports referring to some of the Croat communities to the east and to the north of the provinces or the districts you have marked in red here. So, yes, we tried our very best to understand the composition of the population in the various parts of the territory. Does that answer your question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It does, yes. Thank you. Perhaps just another question. Will you please look at the north-west part of this map marked green, which shows the predominance of predominantly Muslim municipalities of Velika Kladusa, and others. Are you familiar with the name of Fikret Abdic and his political standing, his political activities?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the name of Mr. Abdic, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that Mr. Abdic is a Muslim by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my understanding, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that at some point during the war which was raging in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Abdic, as the political leader of the area that we referred to, which is usually called Cazin's Krajina, that he proclaimed an independent province there, that is, independent of the central government in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we knew that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that as a result, a conflict broke out between Muslim forces loyal to Fikret Abdic and the Muslim forces loyal to the central government and the BH army?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general, yes. I don't think I would be able to give you the precise details of the fighting and the times, but yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So I won't insist on this particular topic anymore, but I should like to ask could we get the number for this exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document will be numbered D49/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us move on to another subject, Mr. Andersen, and that is the relations between the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I assume, and you yourself said, that before you assumed this responsible role, that you, of course, took pains to gather some information about the situation in that part of the world. That is so, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this regard, I should like to ask you to look at a document which has already been tendered here as an exhibit, and I also have copies for you and for the ELMO so we could follow it easier. This is Document D98/1. So this is an agreement on friendship and cooperation between the Republics of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia, and I should like to draw your attention, Mr. Andersen, that evidently there has been an error in this document which was that it was referring to the 21st of July, '91, and it was '92 in fact, because in '91 the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not exist yet. So Mr. Andersen, you must be aware that on the 6th of April, '92, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina proclaimed its independence, its sovereignty. Do you know that in the wake of that, that is, the very next day, the 7th of April, it was the first one to recognise the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that the Republic of Croatia was the first country member of the world community which sent its ambassador to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, while the war was going on in the occupied Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say that I knew for certain that it was the first, but I knew that it was one of the first.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you now please look at Item 3 on page 2 of the document? It says here that the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina expresses its gratitude to the Republic of Croatia for having received and provided for refugees. The ECMM, and you personally, were aware of the fact that the Republic of Croatia, as the war raged in Bosnia-Herzegovina as well as during the war that raged in the Republic of Croatia, offered refuge to some 250.000 Muslim refugees who had escaped to the territory of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general, yes. I'm not quite so certain about the figure, but the order of magnitude seems to be about right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please look at Item 6 on the same document. The ECMM, and you personally, were you aware of the fact that in keeping with this agreement, the HVO became an integral part of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what the document says, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please now look at Item 7. Did you know that under this agreement, the Republic of Bosnia and the Republic of Croatia assumed a mutual or reciprocal obligation to grant dual nationality to their citizens?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general, yes, and I seem to remember that the implementation of it was complicated. But in general, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you please look at page 3 of this document now. I would like to draw your attention to the end of the third section, where it says that the states would continue their cooperation in the military sphere and would coordinate military operations. Were you aware of this agreement?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a memory of it which is sufficiently clear to say "yes", but in general, that was the impression that we had, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So we don't need this document anymore. You said, during your examination-in-chief, Mr. Andersen, that you got some basic impressions. After all, you stayed in Zagreb, the capital of Croatia, so I have a question in relation to that. You personally and the ECMM mission, were you aware of the fact that the Republic of Croatia had passed certain laws whereby the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina would be expelled from its territory? I'm referring to persons of Muslim ethnicity and I'm referring to the period when you were there. Were there any laws that would block their bank accounts, freeze their assets, or something to that effect?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no recollection of having seen any such law or decree, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The International Community, and, of course, through the activity of the ECMM, decided, as you told us, to exert some pressure on the Republic of Croatia through its president, Dr. Tudjman, that he use his influence and try to put a stop to the fighting between the Muslim and Croat communities in Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question would be the following: Was there indeed an attempt made by the Republic of Croatia, through its president, to influence both communities, naturally the Croat community more, but both communities in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and there are numerous examples that would point that out, not to go into all of them now?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the pile of documents brought into evidence, there are communiqués and reports on President Tudjman visiting and talking to Bosnian Croat leaders and to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Andersen, could you please have a look at a document that you already saw during your examination-in-chief? I'm talking about document Z910, 910/1. I have a copy here so you don't have to look through all your documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could the usher please assist me and have this placed on the ELMO and have it distributed as well, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please have a look at page 3 of this document. So, Mr. Andersen, you said during your testimony that on the 24th of April, 1993, a meeting was organised in Zagreb under the patronage of Lord Owen, so to speak. The meeting was attended by Mr. Alija Izetbegovic as the representative of the Muslim community and Mr. Boban as the representative of the Croat community from Bosnia-Herzegovina. President Tudjman had, in a way, given the initiative for calling this meeting. Do you have any information about this?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the information in the documents that you have put before me, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please have a look at another document which was already tendered in this case. This is D33/2. You see an appeal that was addressed by President Tudjman to the Muslim and Croat leaders in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, calling upon them to stop fighting. He also invited them to Zagreb on the 24th of April, 1993, to attend a meeting with Lord Owen. You can see the last line of this document. Is that the meeting that we talked about?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it is, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So let us go back to that meeting and to its aftermath. There was a press release through HINA, the Croat news agency, and it was said that attempts were made to stop the fighting. Is it true that the Croatian parliament established a multi-party delegation with a view to its going to the critical areas in order to bring about a ceasefire?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that there was a delegation formed. I have no clear recollection of whom they met and what the results were, but I remember that the delegation was discussed and I believe it was formed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it jog your memory if I said that in Bosnia, unfortunately, it was not possible for this delegation to visit these critical areas?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that is the term in one of the ECMM reports, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Andersen, that President Tudjman, during his visit to Turkey, which is also a predominantly Muslim republic in terms of the ethnic background of the population and religious, that an agreement was reached to set up a governmental commission between Croatia and Turkey that would be sent to Bosnia as a goodwill mission?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that President Tudjman also talked to the highest representative of the Islamic community in Croatia and Slovenia and asked him to influence his Muslim believers to the effect of having the fighting stopped in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way you're asking the questions, it calls for a more or less yes or no. Yes, I was aware of it, but if you'll allow me the further comment that I've already made before, that in many cases in the former Yugoslavia, people had more than one agenda. I think that is also a remark to cover the activities of President Tudjman. He's on record, as you have stated here, of appealing to the various parties. He's on record of having met with the Turkish representatives and Muslim representatives in Croatia and Slovenia. That, I think, is one of the agendas, to be seen to exert influence. It was our assessment that in order for this agenda to be the prevailing one, there was still a need for some prodding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood your answer correctly, Mr. Andersen, in spite of these efforts the conflicts did not stop in the area, in Bosnia and Herzegovina, is that right, at least at that time?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conflict did not stop at that time. It went up and down but it didn't stop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know, Mr. Andersen, that you left your post sometime in July 1993. However, I'm going to ask you something about the following: Do you know something about the agreement from the 30th of July, 1993, between the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia, so to speak, and this agreement resulted in a joint declaration between Presidents Tudjman and Izetbegovic in Geneva in September 1993? Do you know about this joint declaration?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of it. I have no precise information on what went on there -- I had left the mission and I was preparing for another assignment -- but in general, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Andersen, could you please have a look at the text of this joint declaration and tell me whether that is the document that we've just been discussing?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I would like to have it admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is numbered D50/2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. Andersen, I'm not going to ask you about the document itself because it's self-explanatory; however, I would like to hear your comment. Is that the meeting we discussed which was a consequence of the Geneva agreements between Izetbegovic and Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I believe, but as we have talked about, I wasn't there at the time. I was preparing for another assignment, so I didn't follow events closely enough to have any specific opinion on this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Andersen, for having been patient with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If the usher could leave the last document, perhaps we should start with that. Re-examined by Mr. Scott:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The document which is Exhibit D50/2, looking at this document, sir, this appears to be essentially what might be considered a peace agreement or ceasefire involving Bosnia in terms of the conflict between the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims. Does that appear to be the case from looking at the document?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would, but I mean, there are no signatures, there are markings, et cetera. So whether this was the actual final document is difficult to say. It could be a draft. It could have been signed. I think it was signed, but I mean ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Assuming for the moment -- putting aside the ultimate authenticity of the document and whether this was ever signed or not, which we can perhaps suspend for the moment, this, though, was an agreement to resolve a conflict that at least by some accounts was, some would suggest, and certainly Croatia had suggested, was purely internal to Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, signed by President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, and that was my question. But to resolve an agreement, by his account wholly internal to Bosnia-Herzegovina, but the two parties signing it was the president of that country and, in fact, Mr. Tudjman, the president of the wholly third country or foreign country; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And that is consistent with what the ECMM held for true, that the Republic of Croatia was an important factor in the events of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've said a few moments ago that Mr. Tudjman's visits to various places such as Turkey and other public appearances for the purposes of being seen to support a peace effort concerning Bosnia was considered by ECMM to be one of his agendas. Can you tell the Court what might have been his other agenda?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm perhaps overlooking a few, but the one certain agenda could be for Croatia to be seen as a country with close ties to the West and which would ultimately become members of the Western organisations and interlinked in the Western economic system. I think that was one of the paramount interests of President Tudjman and Croatia, and that was one of the reasons why they seceded from the former Yugoslavia. They didn't want to be part of that economic and political system. They wanted, together with Slovenia, to join the north-western part of Europe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you at ECMM sense any conflict between the agenda on the one hand to be seen as, if I can say it this way, a respectable member of the Western European community and on the other hand the desires of the Bosnian Croat leadership to be part of or confederated with Croatia?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it calls more for speculation than for a statement of fact, but there's very little question that Croatia wanted both to the extent possible --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in case of conflict between the aims. I would tend to believe, but others would perhaps defer, but I would tend to believe that Croatia's linkage with the respectable West would have overriding importance to the government and to Dr. Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And staying on President Tudjman for a moment, there was an earlier document, perhaps we can just refer to it without taking the time to pull it out again, Defence Exhibit 27/1, which was the agreement signed between, I think again, Mr. Izetbegovic and Mr. Boban in Zagreb around the 23rd of April, 1993, in which Tudjman also signed it. Well, I think I'm going to have to correct myself. Forgive me. It's probably going to be necessary to look at the document. Defence 27/1. Perhaps we could just look at the third page, signature page, first on the ELMO, if that's possible. Mr. Brix Andersen, if you could let the usher see that momentarily to put it on the ELMO. Thank you. On the third page, just confirming that it was, in fact, signed by Mr. Boban, President Izetbegovic, and President Tudjman. If could I then direct your attention to paragraph 5, starting on page 2 --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, just for the accuracy of the record -- obviously the document speaks for itself -- but I think that to be fair, the question should reflect that Dr. Tudjman witnessed that agreement. He did sign but only as a witness, not as one of the contracting parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No position to the contrary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at paragraph 5, the document states: "The signatories of the joint statement condemn most severely all violations of the rules of International Humanitarian Law regardless of their perpetrators, both sides having been responsible, according to data available so far, and undertake to urgently initiate joint and individual inquest concerning each instance of violation of such rights and immediately examine personal responsibility for the conflicts and crimes perpetrated against the civilian population." Now, sir, would you agree with me that in the wake of the events around Ahmici and the Lasva Valley in April of 1993, there was considerable international pressure, partly reflected back by this document, considerable international tension brought to bear on these atrocities?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a great deal of attention, yes. We wanted that attention also. That was why we sent the three Ambassadors to Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court whether or not as part of this international essentially world class interest, was part of that focus brought on President Tudjman and his government, to try again to use the influence to get some answer to the causes and perpetrators of these atrocities?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the constant aim of the co-chairman and whoever met with President Tudjman and others to see to it that the atrocities were limited in number and scope and that the people who had committed them, they were brought to trial.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, sir, by the time you left the ECMM at the beginning of July, 1993, had any public report or criminal charges been brought or military discipline been exercised, to your knowledge, over any party involved or allegedly involved in carrying out the atrocities in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Concerning the questions about the views of individual monitors, can you tell the Court: Did you ever find Ambassador Thebault to be biased or prejudiced for or against any particular of the parties involved in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I most certainly did not. He was a very competent, very professional French diplomat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Concerning -- there was a series of questions concerning Mr. Kordic's role or position. Do you recall receiving any reports from the field, either from ECMM or UNPROFOR or otherwise, indicating that in any meetings or communications with Mr. Kordic that he expressed a disagreement or rejection of the view that he was, in fact, a powerful and central figure among the Bosnian Croat leadership?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Objection, to the extent that that calls for speculation, Your Honour. That would assume that Mr. Kordic would be aware of the reports that were being made about him by the ECMM, and this witness has stated that those were entirely internal reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The question is allowable. It's an open-ended question and the witness can give a response.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get my question or would you prefer I repeat it, sir?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I would prefer to know exactly what I'm responding to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Let me just simply read it back to you. I'm not sure I can improve on it. Do you recall receiving any reports from the field, either from ECMM or UNPROFOR, otherwise indicating that at any meetings or communications with Mr. Kordic, that he expressed a disagreement or rejection of the view that he was, in fact, a powerful and central figure amongst the Bosnian and Herzegovinian -- actually, if I could correct that to say the Bosnian Croat [realtime transcript read in error "Bosnian and Croatian"] leadership?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw such reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any information that both Mr. Kordic's colleagues, if I can use that term, his fellow members of such things as the HDZ, the HVO, and members of the international organisations in Central Bosnia frequently referred to him as "Colonel Kordic"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, all right, Your Honour. I'm sorry to belabour this, but I think it's important for the transcript. My last question, line 14 of the screen, should be "the Bosnian Croat leadership." Your Honour, if you could give me just one moment, please. Your Honour, I think in the interests of time, and I know the Court does not want us presumably to stand here and read lengthy passages from the documents in evidence, perhaps I can indicate to the Court this: There was a considerable line of questions about the question whether, in fact, Herceg-Bosna was not intended by the Bosnian Croat leadership as a temporary authority ultimately loyal to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There are a series of documents that are already in evidence, and if time allowed and if the Court was so inclined, I could take the witness through them. But I would point the Court to Exhibits Z859,1, Z1013, and Z993, in particular, which I can simply represent to the Court, and I'm happy to go there if the Court wishes me to, deals with this issue at length in which the ECMM's position is that that characterisation of Herceg-Bosna is not accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could just maybe close on this point, Your Honour, and then I have only one other point to make.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brix Andersen, if I can direct your attention to Exhibit 1065, your, as you've called it several times, your valedictory report, do you have that still? Perhaps if you could keep your finger on that for one moment, 1065, and then could you also find and have in front of you Exhibit 1061. It's actually just the document immediately before it, I believe. Sorry if that's unwieldy, but if you would look first at Exhibit 1061, to the fourth page where you testified yesterday about the four aims of the HVO. Do you have that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the time that your tenure ended in early July of 1993, did you and ECMM see that the HVO views or aims had changed in any significant respect from those four aims or did they continue to be the same?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's my belief and my understanding of it that they were still the aims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, in fact, if you will look then at 1065 very briefly, Your Honours, to page 2, carrying over to the top of page 3, do you not at those locations in many respects reaffirm and restate those same aims?

utterances.speaker: OLE BRIX ANDERSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In terms of the friendship or cooperation agreement that Mr. Cerkez's counsel showed you, in terms of military cooperation, let me -- if we can hopefully do it shortly this way: Was it ECMM's assessment, again at least continuing up until the time that you left that organisation, that the State of Croatia and its armed forces were not involved in Bosnia, only in connection with fighting against what might be called the Serb forces, but that the State of Croatia and its armed forces were also involved in supporting and involved in the armed conflict between the Bosnian Croats and the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Objection to the leading nature of that question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, this is an International Tribunal. We are not in some national jurisdiction where we have to have these constant interruptions. But it doesn't help, equally, if leading questions are asked. Counsel should be experienced enough not to do that. Now, is that concluding the witness's evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I can ask that several different ways but I'm trying to be sensitive to the time factor. I would be happy to take the Court's guidance either way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we've had this question answered several times. We don't need to hear it again. Mr. Brix Andersen, thank you for your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. Your evidence is now concluded, and you're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I've just got this manila bundle. I wondered whether it's going to be of use when the witness gives evidence next week or whether it's intended to produce yet another bundle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think we're undecided on that yet, and we probably won't be able to decide until the end of Monday. But can we keep it in mind, and if we keep that manila bundle to hand, we'll try and remember either to say, "That's the bundle to use," or, "There's a substitute bundle."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. And if we can use the same one, so much the better.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I absolutely agree. I think it would be sensible to use the same bundle. Your Honour, it's 10 to 1.00. The next witness is the subject of an application in respect of protection, so at some stage we perhaps should go into private session. I have doubts -- I'm going too fast. I have doubts about the wisdom of starting this witness. Perhaps we can go into private session and I'll explain why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We won't start the witness, in any event.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. If we can go into private session, I can deal with the application and a couple of administrative matters as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 1.00 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 2nd day of December, 1999, at 9.30 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
